# <a id="3e5d65dd82be80f0ae2bc5554786b6b0" />Abstract

<Callout icon="">
  <a id="3fdd65dd82be800fa6b1eca1360f5bcd" />As our project this year was to develop an *E. coli* promoter-GFP biosensor, we sought to identify high quality promoters—characterized by dynamic range, low basal expression, and low cross-activation—that enable quantifying presence of antibiotic in solution. Our biosensor depends on a promoter that produces a strong, rapid, and specific fluorescence when a relevant antibiotic is present, therefore promoter performance is critical to the success of FAST’s accuracy: a leaky promoter would yield false susceptibility calls, a slow promoter would reduce our advantage over culture-based testing, etc. However, rather than relying solely on literature review, we wanted to validate our findings through a library screen. We screened a promoter-GFP library against four antibiotics: Amoxicillin, Cephalexin, Gentamicin, and Tobramycin. These antibiotics were chosen as they are β-lactams and aminoglycosides, pertinent to our project for their clinical relevance to UTIs.

  <a id="3fdd65dd82be80cfa295f1cb77877fc7" />To characterize over 200 promoter candidates, we developed the experimental design of a high-throughput experiment executed in collaboration with Biofactorial, an automation facility. Our experiment consisted of three components: assay development, the library screen, then sequencing. By exposing the promoter library to each antibiotic at a selected sub-inhibitory concentration, we collected GFP and $OD_{600}$ measurements and ranked candidates based on sustained induction, response speed, and low baseline expression. Through our criterion we were able to identify the top ten promoters from the library, and sequenced the top candidates back to its well for further validation.
</Callout>

<a id="3fdd65dd82be8087975be726f6e6e36e" />

# <a id="3e5d65dd82be806ea714f7a90e71d3c3" />**Background**

<a id="3fad65dd82be80eaa5fcdacf471b1be4" />Before beginning any experimental planning, we conducted thorough literature review on various aspects to guide our planning. We began by researching top promoter candidates with our desired characteristics to form an idea of expected candidates. The criteria we were looking for is as follows:

<a id="3ffd65dd82be801088eaf82f8edab14a" />

|                                                             |                                       |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| <a id="3ffd65dd82be80afb34dd7e130bf391f" />Criterion        | Requirement                           |
| <a id="3ffd65dd82be805b8ca3cd27f32b2445" />Basal Expression | Low and stable in untreated cultures  |
| <a id="3ffd65dd82be80b1a7d0f5cbd7928677" />Fold Induction   | At least two-fold during screening    |
| <a id="3ffd65dd82be80ff8129c4bb7cdfe158" />Absolute Output  | Clearly above promoterless background |

# <a id="3e5d65dd82be8079af05c75febc5617c" />Method

<a id="3e8d65dd82be80878d35e3da3a754df1" />The objective of the Promoter Library was to identify top promoter candidates out of a library of over 200 promoter candidates. The library consisted of promoter-GFP constructs on well plates. The antibiotic response of these constructs were unknown, as well as the promoter barcodes. Our experiment consisted of three parts: an assay development to select sub-inhibitory concentrations for each antibiotic, the high-throughput library screen exposing the promoter-GFP plates to the antibiotics at the selected concentrations, and then finally Oxford Nanopore sequencing the top candidates. As we had over 200 promoter candidates, doing this experiment on our own bench top would not be effective. Thus, we collaborated with Biofactorial, a High-Throughput Biology and Automation Facility here at UBC’s Life Sciences Institute. Biofactorial was able to execute the assay testing and library screen for us, so we worked in collaboration to develop the proposal and experimental design.

<a id="3fcd65dd82be80bdb51cf62054830b9f" />**Note: complete protocols can be found under** [**Wet Lab - Lab Notebook**](/ubc-vancouver/wet-lab/lab-notebook/biofactorial-part-1-mic-assay)

## <a id="3f9d65dd82be8014888ace9e8aff5203" />**Part 1: Identifying Sub-inhibitory Concentrations**

<a id="3f9d65dd82be80958a9eeb4fa987baf4" />Before beginning the library screen, it was critical to first develop an assay to select sub-inhibitory concentrations for each antibiotic that we would expose the library to during the subsequent screening. We used literature minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values as a reference point for our experimental design, creating a dilution series around the literature MIC values to capture a curve.  Literature review was also conducted on all of the antibiotics to ensure solubility at low concentrations.

<br id="3fad65dd82be8064ba45fdc5e504e0a4" />

<a id="3fad65dd82be80aeb1f2d04b61d579d5" /><u>Two-fold Dilution Series (µg/mL) for Each Antibiotic</u>

<a id="3fad65dd82be805b99e5e186a9928d3d" />

| <a id="3fad65dd82be808699c0fe152547a05b" />Antibiotic  |         |        |       |      |     |    |    |    |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------- | ------ | ----- | ---- | --- | -- | -- | -- |
| <a id="3fad65dd82be80c69fb0ffb19b4a6772" />Amoxicillin | 0.25    | 0.5    | 1     | 2    | 4   | 8  | 16 | 32 |
| <a id="3fad65dd82be80e49bf3cb6a5cb892a2" />Cephalexin  | 0.5     | 1      | 2     | 4    | 8   | 16 | 32 | 64 |
| <a id="3fad65dd82be80c98281cede73399c2c" />Gentamicin  | 0.03125 | 0.0625 | 0.125 | 0.25 | 0.5 | 1  | 2  | 4  |
| <a id="3fad65dd82be80b8b0a9d1ef6b012146" />Tobramycin  | 0.0625  | 0.125  | 0.25  | 0.5  | 1   | 2  | 4  | 8  |

<a id="3f9d65dd82be806ba234eade70507f26" />Each *E. coli* strain from the plates were scraped and grown in LB media tubes overnight. The four antibiotics were also prepared at their subsequent stock volumes. In order to align compatibility with Biofactorial’s operations and equipment, we required setting up our experiment through an antibiotic source place which would then dispense the antibiotic from lowest to highest concentration into a destination plate with the *E. coli*, using a piece of equipment called the Echo Acoustic Liquid Handler. 25 µL of antibiotic was dispensed into each well, and for all experiments we used 384-well plates for consistency. The plate layouts are as follows:

<br id="3fdd65dd82be80f4be58c59657eb5cd6" />

<a id="3e8d65dd82be80cd8754f106221b3177" />Over the duration of 8 hours, $OD_{600} $ was measured every 30 minutes along with GFP fluorescence with 488 nm excitation and detected at 510 nm emission.

### <a id="3ffd65dd82be8020bbb3de8981577d55" />Discussion

<a id="3ffd65dd82be802a8c3ee9a2df42351b" />From the [resulting measurements](/ubc-vancouver/wet-lab/lab-notebook/biofactorial-part-1-mic-assay) we were able to create $OD_{600}$ graphs to visualize the growth inhibition and derive an apparent MIC value, combined with our preliminary knowledge from the literature review.

<a id="400d65dd82be8015b6e7ef674010badb" />Note:

- <a id="400d65dd82be806b807cd7f38b36d31a" />1b represents Plate 1, well A24
- <a id="400d65dd82be800eaf78c70ab725b56b" />1t represents Plate 1, well A1
- <a id="400d65dd82be80739db9fc3799bd2bb0" />2t represents Plate 2, well A1
- <a id="400d65dd82be802ea308dae4cb1daf21" />5 represents Plate 5, well A24
  <br id="400d65dd82be8040b151ca985d49c499" />

<a id="3ffd65dd82be8053a5adff9a2967a2b9" />

<Figure imgs={[{"url":"https://static.igem.wiki/teams/6279/wiki/assets/6c72feca22e45a7ca0844c625a14b053.svg","alt":"","scale":0}]}>
  <Fragment slot="content">
    <a id="3ffd65dd82be8022a79dd760f6ac60eb" />Graphs for each antibiotic comparing concentration level against amount of endpoint growth
  </Fragment>
</Figure>

<a id="3ffd65dd82be802ca6e6eaff95460b18" />From here, we chose our sub-inhibitory concentrations by using roughly 0.25-0.5x the MIC value. We reasoned that this range would be high enough to observe measurable stress on the cells while remaining low enough that growth is not substantially inhibited. Additionally, the selected sub-inhibitory concentrations were consistent with literature. Using this logic we selected one concentration for each antibiotic that we would expose the entire library to in part 2 of our experiment.

| <a id="3ffd65dd82be80169301ed945051cd47" />Amoxicilin | 2                                    |
| <a id="3ffd65dd82be807d91bcca506e407fb8" />Cephalexin | 1                                    |
| <a id="3ffd65dd82be80dd8879d8b64037e37a" />Gentamycin | 1                                    |
| <a id="3ffd65dd82be80348a3bed6f3df0ec10" />Tobramycin | 1                                    |

  </Fragment>

  </Fragment>

  </Fragment>

## <a id="3e5d65dd82be807eabedf015927c482f" />**Part 2: High-throughput Library Screen**

<a id="3e5d65dd82be8082b49fd23996e892d8" />The objective of part 2 was to now conduct the entire library screen by exposing all promoter-GFP constructs to the antibiotics at the selected concentration levels determined from part 1. This required creating 5 replicates of the library plates, so we could expose the library to each of the four antibiotics while having one control plate with no antibiotic exposure. In total, we had 30 plates. Biofactorial was able to carry out the plate replication for us, however, the library plates were not compatible with the Echo Acoustic Liquid Handler. Instead, an alternative pinning machine was used, but this could only dispense 70 nL rather than the original 50 nL of our *E. coli* cells. This simply meant that our starting $OD_{600}$ was slightly higher, but this did not impact our results. From here, the *E. coli* plates were incubated with LB media and the antibiotic for 8 hours, following the same data collection guidelines as part 1: measure $OD_{600}$ every 30 minutes along with GFP fluorescence with 488 nm excitation and detected at 510 nm emission.

### <a id="3ffd65dd82be8032821ef51a515ccfc5" />Discussion

<a id="3ffd65dd82be800791e1c61ba62fa9ff" />From the results collected, the following weighted decision matrix (WDM) was used to screen for the top candidates:

<a id="3ffd65dd82be8008bf1ec8fb34893384" />

|                                                                   |            |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- |
| <a id="3ffd65dd82be80fd9a62ce833fec7822" />Criterion              | Weight (%) |
| <a id="3ffd65dd82be803ea6a4f472125926b3" />Sustained GFP Increase | 45         |
| <a id="3ffd65dd82be80a08bf3dfff3b8c6e79" />Response Speed         | 25         |
| <a id="3ffd65dd82be808385dae86847af47be" />Low Untreated GFP      | 30         |

<a id="400d65dd82be80e7940dcd3188067b64" />

<Figure imgs={[{"url":"https://static.igem.wiki/teams/6279/wiki/assets/ed2a6a573ee65f7bbe271cb664399237.svg","alt":"","scale":0}]}>
  <Fragment slot="content">
    <a id="400d65dd82be800e9288f70d969b06b1" />Visualization of the entire promoter library’s growth and GFP induction, categorized by antibiotic and identifying the top 10 candidates
  </Fragment>
</Figure>

<a id="400d65dd82be804abdddc8b4b5aa6435" />The above graph was produced by normalizing each promoter’s GFP response by $OD_{600}$ and its control. Using the above graph, we can derive a handful of conclusions. First, most of the promoters are clouded around growth = 1 and GFP induction = 1, meaning most of the library was unaffected by the sub-inhibitory concentrations. However, the top candidates are recognizable as they are outliers. The top candidates were hits with high GFP induction (\~ 3x to 12x), with the top hit being 11.68x induction under Amoxicillin. We can also see that majority of the top candidates were for Cephalexin, especially without inhibiting growth (candidates lie more within the right side of the cloud). On the other hand, Tobramycin lies mostly to the lower left, meaning growth is slowed and GFP is lower per cell. Amoxicillin is mostly induced without slowing growth.

<br id="400d65dd82be803b9ba1e36c2603ae86" />

<a id="400d65dd82be809ba680ec392f5e4609" />However, given that the library was initially on 96-well plates and had been re-mapped onto our 384-well plate, we also needed to account for this. Through this theory, each single well in the 96-well plate corresponds to a 2x2 block of four wells in the 384-well plate. Therefore we aimed for 4 wells from each 2x2 quadrant across the 384-well plate. Furthermore, we deliberately picked four wells from plate 6 (one from each quadrant) to determine the quadranting order.

### <a id="3ffd65dd82be806f8147f222d6ce182b" />Results

<a id="3fad65dd82be80699423deb7d5bf5719" />The top 10 promoter candidates from the library based on our desired profile and taking into consideration the re-mapping are as follows:

<a id="400d65dd82be80d1ae1af8cc9e28f716" />

|                                                    |                |             |
| -------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | ----------- |
| <a id="400d65dd82be807b9450f01a82d5fdb0" />Ranking | Promoter       | Antibiotic  |
| <a id="400d65dd82be80ecbd64e9811b785bfb" />1       | Library 6, G20 | Amoxicillin |
| <a id="400d65dd82be80eb8ffdf2b8ec3afba3" />2       | Library 6, G17 | Cephalexin  |
| <a id="400d65dd82be80699883c12f267ce416" />3       | Library 6, M12 | Amoxicillin |
| <a id="400d65dd82be80fb8678eef31a2481ae" />4       | Library 6, B5  | Cephalexin  |
| <a id="400d65dd82be80f48ef5cb304c6c04b5" />5       | Library 6, L9  | Tobramycin  |
| <a id="400d65dd82be807c888bc643811818cd" />6       | Library 6, K15 | Amoxicillin |
| <a id="400d65dd82be8058964bd9912a3851cc" />7       | Library 1, G3  | Cephalexin  |
| <a id="400d65dd82be8069acbdfda0689ee8e3" />8       | Library 6, B9  | Cephalexin  |
| <a id="400d65dd82be8057bd04f008b8bf32f9" />9       | Library 6, N9  | Cephalexin  |
| <a id="400d65dd82be80c6967eecb86d33f352" />10      | Library 6, J12 | Cephalexin  |

<a id="21416bfb949d4484b0fca024589755b4" />

<a id="8256df8032f54e2f8a3c3c52fee27d3e" />

<Dbtl>
  <Fragment slot="design">
    <a id="eb86b34d21b84ef7add4fcb4b9e1cd37" />Now that we’ve identified the concentration we want to test each antibiotic at, we can begin designing the well plate layouts.
  </Fragment>

  <Fragment slot="build">
    <a id="fa92a2fde50c4536933961cde646d591" />Biofactorial assists us in setting up the experiment by replicating the library plate 5x, and preparing the plates with LB media and each corresponding antibiotic
  </Fragment>

  <Fragment slot="test">
    <a id="bf08856b8bad414ebb6be7619adb0e9e" />Now, the plates are ran for 8 hours, collecting $OD_{600}$ and GFP fluorescence measurements at 30 minute time points
  </Fragment>

  <Fragment slot="learn">
    <a id="a1b94eb9e7e545fe9dc3e0f6979e3689" />Using our readouts, we compare each antibiotic’s GFP readout to its own control well, as well as normalize GFP to $OD_{600}$ to derive each promoter’s response to each antibiotic
  </Fragment>
</Dbtl>

<br id="3fad65dd82be80a7b998c0c7eef81de9" />

## <a id="3f9d65dd82be80ce99cef1e9a1f08f4c" />**Part 3: Oxford Nanopore Sequencing**

<a id="3ffd65dd82be806c9fa5cf1a15218c6f" />The last step of our experiment was now to map the selected top 10 promoter candidates to their original 96-well plate. We inoculated and grew all 10 candidates however only 7 candidates grew properly, leaving us limited in our scope. Nonetheless, we sent all 7 viable candidates for sequencing. Our sequencing was carried out by Plasmidsaurus, a sequencing company who perform long-read sequencing. From Plasmidsaurus we obtained sequencing results for candidates 1, 4, and 7 in the form of GeneBank files.

### <a id="3ffd65dd82be8038bd0ed0cd49ff3b47" />Discussion

<a id="400d65dd82be80cebb69e9140030a2b4" />To analyze the GeneBank files, we compared the assemblies to find variable insertions by comparing it against the *E. coli* K-12 MG1655 reference genome. Upon doing so, we found that candidates 1 and 4 had the same insert, and matched the region between malE and malK (maltose transport genes). Candidate 7 matched the region between kup (a potassium transporter) and rbsD (ribose metabolism). From here we can use the insert’s position relative to GFP to infer the reporter-facing gene.

### <a id="3ffd65dd82be807e8695e35e49e48264" />Results

<a id="3ffd65dd82be80559517e54e44386523" />

<Figure imgs={[{"url":"https://static.igem.wiki/teams/6279/wiki/assets/2b40cf95fcb85fac9d580c827c9601e5.svg","alt":"","scale":0}]}>
  <Fragment slot="content" />
</Figure>

<a id="3ffd65dd82be80b5b27cc0e3414f704c" />In the figure above we can see that Cephalexin is the only antibiotic that increased GFP induction in all three candidates. On the other hand, Gentamicin and Tobramycin reduced GFP induction, and Amoxicillin leaves Tube 7 almost unchanged. One caveat however, is that if Tube 1 and 7 are identical regions, then their map should look very similiar. Although general similarity can be concluded in Amoxicillin, Cephalexin, and Gentamicin, Tobramycin resulted in opposite induction directions between the two candidates. So, the overall pattern matches in 3 out of 4 conditions. The mixed result in Tobramycin can be a result of various potential factors, ranging from measurement noise to even where the well was position within the plate.

<br id="3e5d65dd82be80abb6f8edee810f78af" />

<a id="3e5d65dd82be80319ec6c478158d34f4" />

<Dbtl>
  <Fragment slot="design">
    <a id="3ebd65dd82be80d18727f00709d736ba" />We used a WDM to rank candidates based on sustained induction, response speed, and low baseline expression. We then designed sampling to account for top candidates as well as the arraying of the 96-well plates re-mapped onto the 384-well plate.
  </Fragment>

  <Fragment slot="build">
    <a id="3ebd65dd82be80bfb86ccbe8429cb7d9" />The selected candidates were inoculated, cultured, and grown. The tubes were sent to Plasmidsaurus for long-read sequencing.
  </Fragment>

  <Fragment slot="test">
    <a id="400d65dd82be80fbb259f4067371f546" />We analyzed the resulting GeneBank files, comparing the assemblies against the plasmid backbone to isolate the variable insertions, then aligned each insert to the *E. coli* MG1655 reference genome. We then used each insert’s position and orientation relative to GFP to infer the likely reporter-facing gene.
  </Fragment>

  <Fragment slot="learn">
    <a id="3ebd65dd82be80f69979e21c3d38f272" />We found that the malE-malK region appeared twice among the three sequenced candidates, and candidate 7 matched the kup-rbsD region.
  </Fragment>
</Dbtl>

<br id="3e8d65dd82be809d993cc363e0bee96c" />

<br id="3e5d65dd82be80f0b1abd2d4c159f5ce" />

# <a id="3e8d65dd82be80e4970cf11676387a74" />**Iterations**

<a id="3fcd65dd82be801e83f5dba024111211" />Throughout all parts of our experiment conducted with Biofactorial, we consulted thoroughly with the Biofactorial lab manager for feedback on our experimental design to ensure it was both feasible in terms of execution, but also would produce the most reliable results. Whether it was during the development of our protocol or last minute adaptations during testing, all decisions reflected our pursuit for reliability and accuracy.

<br id="400d65dd82be8061be79d100411d5e74" />

<a id="400d65dd82be80ea9ef7dd64d97c75b6" />When designing our protocol, we sought feedback on design considerations like how many source wells to use in our subset in part 1 to ensure we were accurately representing the entire library, or how many concentration levels to test to capture a complete antibiotic concentration curve. On the other hand, we also received valuable feedback on the feasibility of our design, like learning how to design a CSV for the antibiotic source plate, or what equipment at Biofactorial’s facility would be most compatible for our experiment. We held meetings with the lab manager as needed, and iterated our experimental design to ensure we would be confident in its results.

<br id="400d65dd82be80a09d0cef15c09f64ba" />

<a id="400d65dd82be8060b09dc1be5fbb7225" />We also made sure to document any changes and decisions made throughout our design process; our [experimental protocols](/ubc-vancouver/wet-lab/lab-notebook/biofactorial-part-1-mic-assay) reflect the final version of our protocol that was performed by Biofactorial.

# <a id="3fcd65dd82be806c8729e1abcaac83d4" />Errors, Limitations, and Future Work

<a id="400d65dd82be8047b929d2b42190fcef" />**Errors**

<a id="400d65dd82be80b6b63fc8a73e77be91" />Our experimental outputs came out generally as expected until we reached sequencing. The first error we ran into was growing the cultures of the top 10 candidates, resulting in only 7 successful inoculations. As a result, this limited the range of promoters we could sequence. Furthermore, upon receiving the GeneBank files from Plasmidsaurus, only candidates 1, 4, and 7 were successfully sequenced. Therefore we ultimately only determined sequencing for 3 promoters. The remaining samples generated sequencing data but were unable to assemble a plasmid sequence. This can be attributed to a variety of reasons such as if there are multiple plasmids in one sample, or if the structure is unusually complex.

<br id="400d65dd82be80089bf3f878f33c0be3" />

<a id="400d65dd82be8084aaf7d54f7cc87654" />**Limitations**

<a id="400d65dd82be80569e60fd9a2e1c2eb9" />Ultimately, various limitations affect the confidence in our conclusions. First, our final promoter sample size was small. Only three candidates were successfully sequenced, and although the malE-malK region appeared twice among them, this is too few data points to generalize to the broader promoter library. Furthermore, determining the reporter-facing gene of the three promoters was done through inference (from the insert’s position relative to GFP) and was not experimentally validated. So, further testing would strengthen these conclusions. Third, some of our assumptions throughout the project can be subjective. For example, the weighting in the WDM used to select top promoter candidates was based on our own individual team’s needs, and could produce a different ranking under a different team’s priorities. Lastly, any noise or interference with the measurements collected from the library screen would carry through to our selection and characterization of top candidates.

<br id="400d65dd82be80f19fd0d1515fe6ebbc" />

<a id="3e8d65dd82be80bd9608e9da7e045123" />**Future Work (addressing our errors)**

<a id="400d65dd82be807bbc49e46d9965ffcc" />Due to time constraints we were not able to carry out our troubleshooting, but we have identified the steps we would like to take to continue building upon this. To continue refining our results, particularly the sequencing aspect, we would like to re-prep and re-sequence the remaining candidates from the top 10. If the failed assembly were in fact a result of mixed colonies, re-streaking can ensure a fresh culture is grown from the new isolated colony. If re-prepping were not an option (as re-sending our samples to a sequencing company can have time or financial constraints) it would also be useful to locate a reference backbone to aid the failed sequences and troubleshoot from there. Lastly, to strengthen confidence in measurements from the library screen, sequencing additional clones and/or replicating the screen can increase reliability. Ultimately, we hope to continue sequencing and mapping more of the promoter library to expand our range of top candidates, in addition to determining more of the 96-well to 384-well plate mapping.
